hops.title: Sponge cells that sort themselves out of a soup
hops.text: In 1907 the biologist Henry Wilson broke up a living marine sponge, Microciona prolifera (now Clathria prolifera), into a loose suspension of cells, and the cells reassembled into a working sponge. Later researchers gently rotated loose cells from two sponge species together in seawater. No hybrid formed: the cells clumped separately by species, with no gradient imposed. Sugars on each species' surface adhesion molecules stick most strongly to the same species' sugars. In 2004, plain lab beads coated with those purified sugars mostly clumped by species of origin too.

sources.citation: Ruperti F, et al. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2024;121(52):e2409125121.
Bucior I, Scheuring S, Engel A, Burger MM. Carbohydrate-carbohydrate interaction provides adhesion force and specificity for cellular recognition. J Cell Biol. 2004;165(4):529-537.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two glass dishes on a wooden bench: one with mixed orange-red and pale yellow sponge cells, the other with the cells regrouped into separate clumps by color.
image.caption: Cells from two sponge species, mixed in seawater, clump back apart by species using species-matched surface sugars.

hops.afterHeading: Same problem, different molecules: the mouse
hops.title: The octopus has 168 protocadherin genes
hops.text: Fruit flies have no protocadherin genes at all, and fellow molluscs such as oysters and limpets carry about 17 to 25. The 2015 genome of the California two-spot octopus turned up 168, nearly three-quarters of them lined up in side-by-side clusters. Counting all 168, that is nearly three times the 58 genes in the mouse's clustered set. An octopus has plenty of wiring to keep sorted: by an estimate from the common octopus, its central brain, optic lobes and arm nerve cords hold nearly half a billion neurons, more than six times a mouse brain. Octopuses and vertebrates expanded this gene family independently.

sources.citation: Albertin CB, et al. The octopus genome and the evolution of cephalopod neural and morphological novelties. Nature. 2015;524(7564):220-224.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A mottled octopus on sandy seafloor with its eight arms spread out and curling, none of them tangled.
image.caption: The California two-spot octopus carries 168 protocadherin genes, nearly three times the mouse's clustered set of 58.

hops.afterHeading: A receptor that is also an address: smell
hops.title: How Broca helped cement the weak human nose myth
hops.text: A common belief is that humans have a poor sense of smell. In 2017 neuroscientist John McGann traced its modern anatomical version not to smell tests but largely to nineteenth-century anatomist Paul Broca, who linked our proportionally small olfactory bulbs to the evolution of free will. The measurements disagree. Human bulbs hold a similar number of neurons to other mammals' bulbs, and volunteers can follow an outdoor scent trail, helped by comparing what each nostril picks up. A mouse sends each receptor's neurons to about two glomeruli per bulb; by 2008 estimates, human bulbs averaged over 5,500 glomeruli against about 350 intact receptor genes, roughly 16 to one.

sources.citation: McGann JP. Poor human olfaction is a 19th-century myth. Science. 2017;356(6338):eaam7263.
Porter J, et al. Mechanisms of scent-tracking in humans. Nat Neurosci. 2007;10(1):27-29.
Maresh A, Rodriguez Gil D, Whitman MC, Greer CA. Principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb: implications for odor processing. PLoS ONE. 2008;3(7):e2640.

image.caption: Broca helped cement the weak human nose myth, yet people can follow a scent trail across a lawn.
